## Desk answer

**Setup.** The book marks at 1,000.4M with a daily mean of -0.10% (-0.00097) and daily volatility of 2.33% (0.02326). Under the normal, iid-per-day assumption the loss quantile is VaR = V·(z·σ − μ)·√h, and the 95% expected shortfall is ES = V·(σ·φ(z)/(1−a) − μ)·√h. All figures below come straight from the fact pack; no tool call was needed.

**VaR results.**
- 1-day 95% VaR: 39.248M
- 1-day 99% VaR: 55.095M
- 10-day 95% VaR: 124.114M (1-day 39.248 × square-root-of-10 scaling 3.1623)
- 10-day 99% VaR: 174.225M (1-day 55.095 × 3.1623)

**95% expected shortfall.** The 1-day 95% ES is 48.957M — that is the average loss inside the worst 5%, sitting above the 1-day 95% VaR of 39.248M, i.e., the tail beyond the VaR threshold is materially deeper than the quantile itself. The 10-day 95% ES scales by the same square-root-of-horizon factor 3.1623 (48.957 × 3.1623).

**What the normality assumption is hiding.** A normal, iid-per-day model assumes symmetric, thin-tailed returns with no serial dependence. An equity long-only book does not behave that way: real returns carry fat tails (extreme moves far more frequent than the normal curve allows), volatility clustering (calm and stormy regimes), and left skew. So the true tail beyond the 95% threshold is worse than the normal ES of 48.957M implies, and the 99% tail is even more understated. The square-root-of-time scaling (3.1623 for 10 days) also rests on iid daily returns; autocorrelation or regime shifts break that link. And note the negative drift (-0.10% daily) is already embedded in these numbers via the −μ term — these are model-implied loss quantiles, not forecasts, and certainly not caps on what the book can lose.

**Abstention.** The 99% expected shortfall over the 10-day horizon is not in the fact pack, so we cannot state it or how far it sits above the 10-day 99% VaR of 174.225M.
